Gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) is a gastrointestinal motility disorder that results from the reflux of stomach contents into the esophagus or oral cavity resulting in symptoms or complications. The typical symptoms of GERD are heartburn and regurgitation of gastric contents into the oropharynx. GERD affects quality of life and may cause erosive esophagitis, esophageal strictures, and Barrett esophagus, a precursor to esophageal adenocarcinoma. GERD is a clinical diagnosis and is most effectively treated with proton-pump inhibitors (PPIs). Long-term use of PPIs is associated with bone fractures, chronic renal disease, acute renal disease, community-acquired pneumonia, and Clostridium difficile intestinal infection.

Gastroesophageal reflux (GER) in children is very common and refers to the involuntary passage of gastric contents into the esophagus. This is often physiological and managed conservatively. In contrast, GER disease (GERD) is a less common pathologic process causing troublesome symptoms, which may need medical management. Apart from abnormal transient relaxations of the lower esophageal sphincter, other factors that play a role in the pathogenesis of GERD include defects in esophageal mucosal defense, impaired esophageal and gastric motility and clearance, as well as anatomical defects of the lower esophageal reflux barrier such as hiatal hernia. The clinical manifestations of GERD in young children are varied and nonspecific prompting the necessity for careful diagnostic evaluation. Management should be targeted to the underlying aetiopathogenesis and to limit complications of GERD. The following review focuses on up-to-date information regarding of the pathogenesis, diagnostic evaluation and management of GERD in children.

Symptoms potentially attributable to gastroesophageal reflux disease are among those most commonly reported to primary care providers in the outpatient setting. In this review, we discuss clinical approaches to the evaluation and management of these symptoms, including proton pump inhibitor trials as well as specific indications or clinical settings that warrant referral to Gastroenterology specialists.

data.narrative: Gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) is a gastrointestinal motility disorder caused by reflux of stomach contents into the esophagus or oral cavity, producing symptoms or complications [18#0]. It is among the most common symptom complexes reported in primary care [20#1]. The hallmark symptoms of GERD are heartburn and regurgitation of gastric contents into the oropharynx [18#2]. In young children, however, clinical manifestations are varied and nonspecific, necessitating careful diagnostic evaluation to distinguish physiological reflux from pathological GERD [19#3]. Multiple mechanisms contribute to GERD development beyond abnormal transient relaxations of the lower esophageal sphincter [19#4]. These include defects in esophageal mucosal defense, impaired esophageal and gastric motility with delayed clearance, and anatomical barrier defects such as hiatal hernia [19#5]. Untreated GERD may lead to erosive esophagitis, esophageal strictures, and Barrett esophagus, which is a precursor to esophageal adenocarcinoma [18#6]. While proton-pump inhibitors are the most effective treatment, their long-term use carries risks including bone fractures, chronic and acute renal disease, community-acquired pneumonia, and Clostridium difficile infection [18#7].

data.narrative: The typical symptoms of GERD are heartburn and regurgitation of gastric contents into the oropharynx [18#0]. GERD is a gastrointestinal motility disorder resulting from reflux of stomach contents into the esophagus or oral cavity [18#1]. Symptoms potentially attributable to GERD are among those most commonly reported to primary care providers in the outpatient setting [20#2]. GERD may cause erosive esophagitis, esophageal strictures, and Barrett esophagus, a precursor to esophageal adenocarcinoma [18#3]. GERD affects quality of life [18#4]. In children, GERD is a pathologic process involving abnormal transient relaxations of the lower esophageal sphincter, defects in esophageal mucosal defense, impaired esophageal and gastric motility and clearance, and anatomical defects such as hiatal hernia [19#5]. Long-term use of PPIs is associated with bone fractures, chronic renal disease, acute renal disease, community-acquired pneumonia, and Clostridium difficile intestinal infection [18#6]. GERD is most effectively treated with proton-pump inhibitors [18#7]. Clinical manifestations of GERD in young children are varied and nonspecific, prompting the necessity for careful diagnostic evaluation [19#8]. The condition is recorded in MedGen as Gastroesophageal reflux (GERD) [2] and is also referred to as Gastroesophageal Reflux [3]. Multiple PubMed publications are titled Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease [1][6][9][15]. One publication addressing pediatric GERD is titled Gastroesophageal reflux disease in children: What's new right now? [12]. Publication pmid 29132520 [5], publication pmid 33351044 [8], publication pmid 36170502 [11], publication pmid 37034973 [14], and publication pmid 37516506 [17] are associated with the GERD literature. A clinical trial named Famotidine in Subjects With Non-erosive Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease [4], a trial named Efficacy of Pantoprazole in Patients Older Than 18 Years Who Have Symptoms of Acid Reflux (Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease) (BY1023/M3-339) [7], a trial named Natural History of Gastroesophageal Reflux (GER) in Children and Adolescents [10], a trial named On Demand Treatment of Reflux Disease [13], and a trial named Treatment Of Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease By Endoscopic Fundoplication, A Placebo-Controlled Study [16] are registered clinical studies addressing GERD treatment and natural history.
